title: 193 Cattle & Climate: Unpacking the science, uncovering the gaps, and exploring ideas for methane mitigation in the Western U.S
content:
Abstract
As concerns over greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and their role in global warming grow, governments worldwide have enacted policies aimed at achieving carbon neutrality. In cattle production, GHG emissions stem primarily from methane (CH₄) produced during digestion and nitrous oxide from manure. Enteric CH₄ is a natural byproduct of anaerobic fermentation in the reticulo-rumen and hindgut of ruminants. The level of CH₄ production is influenced by factors such as feed composition, feed degradation in the rumen, and hydrogen formation during feed breakdown. Thus, cattle diet, and therefore production systems significantly affect GHG emissions. However, long-term studies, particularly those evaluating the practical application of CH₄-mitigators in grazing systems, are limited. Most studies on CH₄ mitigation have focused on additives mixed into a total mixed ration, where supplements are consumed with every bite. There is a scarcity of data on the effectiveness of CH₄-mitigators in supplements provided separately from the basal diet, which cattle may not consume as consistently. To address this gap, it is crucial to evaluate emissions from grazing cattle and assess the effectiveness of additives when supplied as separate supplements. Given that many cattle are raised on rangelands, investigating CH₄-mitigation strategies in these environments is essential. Therefore, our project focuses on evaluating CH₄ emissions from cattle grazing native rangelands on public lands in the Western U.S. from spring to fall, following traditional management practices in this region. Additionally, we are exploring supplementation strategies to reduce CH₄ emissions in these extensive systems. Through outreach efforts, we aim to address general public misconceptions about cattle production and its link to GHG emissions while also helping cattle producers understand possible mitigation strategies.
